subtitle: Long words decoded from the right, and adjectives from suffixes
words.intro: A long German word isn’t hard: it’s a short sentence with the spaces taken out. Read from the right, it explains itself. And there’s no better place to practise than the Autobahn, where the signs arrive at 130 kilometres an hour.

grammar[0].subheading: The joint, decoding from the right, and when it isn’t a genitive
grammar[0].blocks[0].title: The joint
grammar[0].blocks[1].title: Decode from the right
grammar[0].blocks[2].title: Not a genitive
grammar[0].blocks[2].text: The -s- in *Liebesbrief* is a joint: Liebe is feminine and has no genitive -s.
grammar[0].fact: The last word decides everything: the gender, the plural and the meaning. A *Hausschuh* is a shoe, and a *Schuhhaus* is a shop. The little *-s-* in *Geschwindigkeitsbegrenzung* isn’t a genitive, whatever it looks like, and regions disagree on some of them.

grammar[1].subheading: One suffix, one meaning, and those that have drifted
grammar[1].blocks[0].title: One suffix, one meaning
grammar[1].blocks[1].title: Drifted
grammar[1].blocks[1].text: *merkwürdig* means strange, *fragwürdig* questionable. And *sorgenfrei* (carefree) is not *sorglos* (careless).
grammar[1].fact: Once you know the suffix, you can guess the word: *-würdig* (deserves), *-gerecht* (fits), *-bar* (can be), *-frei* (without), *-reich* (with plenty). German advertising adds new ones every year. A product can be *klimaneutral*, *spülmaschinengeeignet*, and *familienfreundlich*, all at once.

document.caption: Am Ortseingang
document.intro: A real sign in Austria, at the entrance to a village. Read the last from the right: *Neben-straßen*, side roads. *Stallhofen* is a compound too, as most German place names are.
document.fact: Place names are compounds, and they’re often very old: *Stall* and *Hof* tell you what people did here. Most German speakers don’t notice, any more than an English person thinks of a ford when they say *Oxford*.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Say what each compound is, starting from the right.
reading.intro: Max and Maya are driving Frau Huber to Hamburg. There’s a traffic jam at Lüneburg. Max has proposed a game, to make the time pass: who can find the longest real word? Frau Huber, in the back with her bag, has said she doesn’t play games.
reading.photos[0].caption: Das Dreieck Karlsruhe: Hier wird es gleich kompliziert.
reading.fact: Frau Huber’s word really existed: it was a state regulation, and it became famous when it was scrapped. So did *Rindfleischetikettierungsüberwachungsaufgabenübertragungsgesetz*, a law on beef labelling. Both were retired, and German lost its record holders. And much of the Autobahn still has no general speed limit, which is itself a national argument.
